question: Is goodness born in people, as Mencius held, or made by training, as Xunzi held?
answer: Anyone who sees a toddler about to fall into a well feels alarm and pity, Mencius argued, before any thought of reward or reputation: goodness has sprouts that need only tending. Modern studies partly agree. In 2006, 18-month-olds picked up objects an adult had dropped and could not reach, unasked and unrewarded, again and again.
move: It turns on whether early kindness or early violence better reveals human nature.
ask: Do I think people are good by nature, and does how I treat them show it?
counterpoint: Human nature is bad, Xunzi wrote; goodness comes from deliberate effort, as warped wood is straightened by steaming and pressing. Children bear him out too: Richard Tremblay's teams, following Canadian children, found hitting, biting and kicking common by 17 months, then fading for most as they grow. Nobody has to teach a toddler to hit.
reference: Hutton (trans.), Xunzi: The Complete Text, Princeton University Press, 2014; Warneken & Tomasello, Altruistic helping in human infants and young chimpanzees, Science 311, 2006; Côté et al., The development of physical aggression from toddlerhood to pre-adolescence, Journal of Abnormal Child Psychology 34, 2006, doi:10.1007/s10802-005-9001-z
